key_terms.meaning: How close a reported fix is to the true position; quoted in metres or nautical miles (1 nm = 1852 m).
How tightly a system repeats the same reading for the same true input; a tight cluster that may still sit off the truth.
The set of all points where one measurement would read the same; two LOPs cross at a fix.
Direction of a station or target from the aircraft, in degrees clockwise from north.
Direction the nose points, in degrees clockwise from north; it is not the same as the track flown.
Earth-Centred Earth-Fixed frame: origin at the Earth's centre, axes rotating with the Earth.
North-East-Down frame at the aircraft: x to north, y to east, z downward along local gravity.
Curve on which the difference of distances to two fixed stations is constant; one hyperbolic LOP.
ILS beam (108.10–111.95 MHz, VHF) that defines the runway centreline in the horizontal plane; full scale is about ±2.5°.
ILS beam (329.15–335.00 MHz, UHF) that defines the vertical approach angle, normally 3°; full scale is about ±0.7°.
Turning of a spin axis at right angles to an applied torque, at the rate Ω = T ÷ H, where H = Iω is the rotor's angular momentum.
Small wobble of the spin axis about its mean direction after a disturbance; it dies out with damping.
Sensor giving the specific force along one axis, in g or m/s²; 1 g = 9.81 m/s².

Giving the inertial loop the 84.4 min period of a pendulum as long as the Earth's radius, so horizontal acceleration does not tilt the platform; errors then oscillate with that period instead of growing freely.
Apparent range c × (receive time − transmit time) from satellite to receiver, wrong by the receiver clock offset, so ρ = r + c δt.
Broadcast orbital parameters that let the receiver compute a satellite's position at a stated time.
Extra path delay from free electrons, 40.3 × TEC ÷ f²: about 1.6 m on L1 for every 10 TEC units, several metres to tens of metres by day, more near the horizon.
Column of the quantities the filter estimates, for example position, velocity and sensor biases.
Square matrix holding the filter's own uncertainty in x; diagonal entries are variances.
GPS pseudo-ranges fed straight into the Kalman filter instead of a pre-computed GPS position.
Automatic Dependent Surveillance–Broadcast: aircraft transmit identity, position and velocity from on-board systems.
FMCW radar at 4.2–4.4 GHz measuring true height above the ground directly below, typically 0–2500 ft.
Warning that compares the projected flight path with a terrain database before the terrain reaches radio-altimeter range.

takeaways: Every navigation system turns a measurement into a line of position; two lines of position make a fix, and a third checks it.
A radio aid is either point source (range or bearing to one station) or hyperbolic (difference of ranges to two stations).
ILS splits the job in two: the localizer owns left and right, the glideslope owns up and down, and the pilot flies the needles.
A spinning mass holds its axis in inertial space, and a torque turns that axis at 90° to the torque at the rate Ω = T ÷ H: that is precession, the basis of every gyro instrument.

An INS integrates its own accelerations, so it is smooth and self-contained; with Schuler tuning its errors swing with an 84.4 min period, but a gyro bias still makes the position error ramp up, about 0.6 nm an hour for 0.01 °/h.
GPS measures travel time, not angle; four satellites are needed because the receiver clock offset is a fourth unknown.
GPS error comes from four families — clocks and orbits, ionosphere, troposphere, local effects — and each family has its own cure.
A Kalman filter weights the drifting INS and the noisy GPS by their covariances, giving a solution better than either alone.
Radar gives range from echo travel time and bearing from antenna pointing; ADS-B shares position by broadcast instead of by echo.
TAWS joins a reactive radio-altimeter layer with a look-ahead terrain-database layer to warn the crew early enough to climb.
bank_note: Long answers here are marked on the geometry and the block diagram: draw the lines of position or the blocks, label every one, then attach the numbers and a closing check, because examiners ask for principle, components and functions together.

bank.q: Define a line of position. Show how a measured range to a station and a measured bearing to a station each produce one line of position on a chart, and how a fix is obtained.
outline: LOP defined as the locus of constant measurement
Range gives a circle centred on the station with radius equal to the range
Bearing gives a straight line radiating from the station (a great circle on the Earth)
Two LOPs intersect at a fix; a third LOP shows the quality of the fix
Cocked hat is drawn around the crossing when errors are present
answer: A line of position (LOP) is the set of all points at which one measurement would give the value actually read. The aircraft must be somewhere on it. A horizontal position has two unknowns, so one LOP is not enough: two LOPs that cross give a fix, and a third one checks it.

answer.text: Each kind of measurement gives its own shape of LOP:

head: Measurement
Typical aid
Line of position
Centre or foci
rows: Straight line (a great circle) out from the station

answer: Range gives a circle. DME measures slant range; after removing the height effect it gives ground range d. Every point d from the station reads the same, so the LOP is a circle centred on the station with radius d. Example: 50 nm from DME station A puts the aircraft somewhere on a circle of radius 50 nm round A.

Bearing gives a straight line. A VOR receiver measures the radial, the magnetic bearing of the aircraft from the station; an ADF measures the relative bearing of an NDB, and adding heading gives the bearing. All points from which the station bears the same direction lie on one line out from the station: on the Earth a great circle, on a chart near the station a straight line. Over long distances the bearing measured at the aircraft and the radial measured at the station differ by the convergence of the meridians, so plot the radial from the station.

answer.text: Two ranges give a fix. DME stations A and B are 130 nm apart; the aircraft reads 50 nm to A and 120 nm to B. Put A at the origin and B on the x-axis:

answer: Two circles cross twice, once on each side of AB, so a two-range fix has an ambiguity; the planned route or a VOR radial picks the right crossing.

answer.text: Range and bearing from one station give a fix. VOR/DME reads radial 060 and 50 nm. The circle and the radial always cross at 90° and only once:
answer.pre:
east of station  = 50 × sin 60° = 43.30 nm
north of station = 50 × cos 60° = 25.00 nm

answer.text: Quality of the fix. Each LOP is uncertain by a band ±σ across it. Two bands overlap in a parallelogram, and the fix error is about σ ÷ sin θ, where θ is the cut angle. With σ = 0.5 nm:

answer: A third LOP and the cocked hat. With small errors, three LOPs do not meet at one point but form a small triangle, the cocked hat. The fix is taken at its centre, and the size of the triangle shows how good the measurements are; a large triangle means one measurement is wrong and should be checked or dropped.

Check: in the two-range example 50² + 120² = 2500 + 14 400 = 16 900 = 130², so the triangle is right-angled at the aircraft, the cut is 90° and the fix error equals the error of one line, the best a two-line fix can do.

bank.q: Distinguish point-source from hyperbolic radio navigation. Name one operational system of each and state exactly what the airborne receiver measures.
outline: Point source: one station, receiver measures range (DME) or bearing (VOR, ADF)
Hyperbolic: two stations, receiver measures time difference which equals a constant difference of distances
Constant difference of distances is a hyperbola with the stations as foci
Three or more stations give a family of hyperbolas and hence a fix
Examples: DME and VOR as point source, Loran-C or Decca as hyperbolic
Rho-theta (VOR/DME) mixes one range and one bearing from the same station
answer: Point-source aids use one ground station per line of position. The airborne set measures something about that station alone: a bearing to or from it, or a range from it. The LOP is a straight line or a circle centred on the station.

Hyperbolic aids use a pair of synchronised stations, a master and a secondary. The receiver measures only the difference in arrival time (or phase) of their signals. A time difference Δt is a range difference Δr = c Δt, and the points with a constant difference of distance to two fixed points form a hyperbola with the stations as foci.

answer.text: The two families side by side:

head: Point source
Hyperbolic
rows: Bearing (phase or direction) or range (round-trip time)
Two pairs: a master and two secondaries

answer: What each receiver measures exactly. ADF: the relative bearing of an NDB (LF/MF, about 190–1750 kHz) from a loop and sense antenna; adding heading gives the bearing. VOR (108–117.95 MHz): the phase difference between a 30 Hz reference signal and a 30 Hz variable signal, which equals the radial. DME (962–1213 MHz): the time from its interrogation to the transponder's reply, less the transponder's fixed 50 µs delay. LORAN-C: the time between the master's and the secondary's pulses, less the secondary's fixed emission delay.

answer.text: DME timing. One nautical mile of range costs 2 × 1852 ÷ c = 12.36 µs of round trip. At 100 nm slant range:
answer.pre:
round trip = 2 × 185 200 ÷ (2.998 × 10⁸) = 1235.5 µs
reply seen after 1235.5 + 50 = 1285.5 µs
range = c × (t − 50 µs) ÷ 2 = 100 nm

answer.text: Hyperbolic working. After the emission delay is removed, the secondary's pulse arrives 100 µs after the master's; the baseline is 600 km:
answer.pre:
Δr = c Δt = 3 × 10⁸ × 100 × 10⁻⁶ = 30.0 km
semi-major axis a = Δr ÷ 2 = 15.0 km
half baseline f = 300.0 km, b = √(300.0² − 15.0²) = 299.6 km
the secondary is farther, so the aircraft is on the branch nearer the master, 15.0 km from the baseline centre

answer: Rho-theta. A VOR with a co-located DME (or a TACAN) gives a bearing line and a range circle from the same point. They always cross at 90°, so one station gives a complete fix with the best possible cut.

Accuracy in use: point-source accuracy is angular for bearings (a fixed angular error spreads with distance) and nearly constant for DME; hyperbolic lines spread apart away from the baseline and on the baseline extension, where fixes are poor. LORAN-C chains gave fixes of a few hundred metres over coastlines and continents.
Check: Δr = 30 km is less than the 600 km baseline, as it must be for a real hyperbola, and 1285.5 µs − 50 µs = 1235.5 µs ÷ 12.36 µs per nm = 100 nm.

bank.q: List the ground and airborne components of ILS and state the function of each, giving the frequency band and the localizer and glideslope widths.
outline: Localizer in the 108–112 MHz band, 90 Hz and 150 Hz tones, full-scale deflection about 2.5° each side of centreline
Glide path in the 329.15–335.00 MHz band, path normally 3°, full-scale deflection about 0.7° each side
Marker beacons at 75 MHz: outer about 4 to 7 nm out, middle about 1 km out (inner markers only at some CAT II/III runways)
Difference in depth of modulation drives the left-right and up-down needles
Airborne receiver, antenna, and display on the attitude director and HSI
Identification by Morse code; approach minima depend on the ILS category
answer: ILS gives a straight, precise approach path in low visibility. Two ground transmitters each define one angle, markers or DME give distance, and the airborne set shows deviations on two needles.

answer.text: Ground and airborne components:

head: Component
Where
Frequency
Function
rows: Beyond the far end of the runway, on the centreline
Left-right guidance along the extended centreline; carries the Morse identifier
About 300 m in from the threshold, beside the runway
Up-down guidance on a slope of usually 3°
Outer about 4 to 7 nm out; middle about 1 km out
Distance check points: outer 400 Hz and blue light, middle 1300 Hz and amber
Co-sited with the glide path or localizer
Continuous slant range, often replacing markers
Switch a transmitter off or to standby if its beam moves out of tolerance
Localizer and glide path receivers tuned together
Deviation pointers on the PFD (or EADI) and HSI; signals to the autopilot

answer: How the guidance is coded. Each beam carries a 90 Hz and a 150 Hz tone in two overlapping lobes. The receiver measures the difference in depth of modulation, DDM = m150 − m90. On the course line DDM = 0 and the needle is centred; the needle deflection is proportional to DDM.

Localizer sense and width. Seen from an approaching aircraft, 90 Hz predominates on the left and 150 Hz on the right. Full scale is DDM 0.155, at the edge of a sector about 2.5° each side; the sector is set to be 210 m (700 ft) wide at the threshold, so a long runway gets a narrower angle.

answer.text: For a localizer 3300 m from the threshold:
answer.pre:
half-angle = arctan(105 ÷ 3300) = 1.82°
full-scale offset at 10 km from the antenna = 10 000 × tan 1.82° = 318 m

answer: Glide path sense and width. 90 Hz predominates above the path and 150 Hz below it. Full scale is DDM 0.175, at about 0.7° above or below a 3° path, so the sector is about 1.4° thick.

answer.text: On the path, 5.0 nm from where it meets the runway:
answer.pre:
5.0 nm = 30 381 ft
height = 30 381 × tan 3° = 1592 ft (about 318 ft per nm)

answer: Tuning and identification. The 40 glide path channels are paired with the localizer channels, so selecting the localizer frequency tunes both. The localizer carries a two- or three-letter Morse identifier, which the crew checks before using the approach; a monitor-tripped beam goes silent rather than giving false guidance.

answer.text: Categories. The ILS category and the aircraft and crew approvals set how low the crew may go before seeing the runway:

head: Category
Decision height
Runway visual range
rows: less than 175 m but not less than 50 m

answer: Check: the two full-scale widths, ±2.5° and ±0.7°, give a sector about 3.6 times wider in azimuth than in elevation, and 318 m at 10 km is 3.03 times the 105 m half-width at the threshold, the ratio of the distances 10 000 ÷ 3300 = 3.03.

bank.q: Explain the principle of a gyroscope and distinguish precession from nutation, stating where each matters in an aircraft instrument.
outline: A spinning mass with angular momentum along its spin axis; axis stays fixed in inertial space
Two degrees of freedom make a free (TDF) gyro for angles; a spring-restrained single-degree gyro measures rate, a damped one integrates rate
Precession: an applied torque turns the spin axis at 90° to the torque, at Ω = T ÷ H with H = Iω
Nutation: transient wobble of the axis after a sudden torque, damped out by the gimbal and the spin
Use in attitude indicator, heading indicator, turn coordinator and in inertial sensors
Gimbal lock and drift limits are practical consequences
answer: Principle. A rotor spinning about its axis carries angular momentum H = Iω along the spin axis. Without torque H cannot change, so the axis keeps its direction in inertial space: rigidity. A torque T changes H at the rate T = dH/dt, and that change is at right angles to H.

answer.text: For a directional gyro rotor with I = 1.2 × 10⁻⁴ kg·m² at 24 000 rpm:

answer: Precession. A steady torque at right angles to the spin axis does not tilt the axis the way the torque pushes. The axis turns about the third axis, at 90° to both the spin and the torque, at the steady rate Ω = T ÷ H. The direction is found by carrying the torque round 90° in the direction of spin. A large H makes Ω small, which is why instrument rotors spin at 20 000 rpm and more.

answer.text: Bearing friction of 5 × 10⁻⁶ N·m on that rotor:

answer: Nutation. When a torque is applied suddenly, the axis does not settle at once into steady precession. It overshoots and traces small, fast loops around the precession path. For a symmetric rotor the loops repeat at about ωn = H ÷ It, where It is the moment of inertia about a gimbal axis. Gimbal friction and damping remove it, leaving pure precession.

answer.text: Taking I<sub>t</sub> = 6.0 × 10⁻⁵ kg·m² for the same rotor (about half of I, as for a thin disc):
Precession against nutation.

head: Precession
Nutation
rows: A steady torque at 90° to the spin axis
A sudden torque or a shock
Steady turn of the axis at Ω = T ÷ H
Fast, small circles about the mean path at about H ÷ I<sub>t</sub>
Used: rate gyro, erection, slaving; unwanted: real drift of the heading indicator
Settling of gyros after a jolt; a rate-gyro damper and stiff gimbals keep it small

answer: Use in instruments. The attitude indicator uses a two-degree-of-freedom vertical gyro, held to the vertical by an erection system that is itself a controlled precession. The heading indicator uses a directional gyro with a horizontal axis; its real drift (here 3.42 °/h) and the apparent drift from the Earth's rotation (15.04 × sin φ °/h, 3.38 °/h at 13° N) mean it is reset to the compass about every 15 minutes. The turn coordinator uses a spring-restrained single-degree rate gyro: the case turns at Ω, the gyro needs a torque HΩ to follow, and the spring deflects by θ = HΩ ÷ k.
Practical limits: gimbal lock when two gimbal axes line up, caging to hold the gimbals square before start or in aerobatics, and real drift from friction and imbalance, which a large H keeps small.

Check: in 15 minutes the heading indicator at 13° N drifts (3.42 + 3.38) × 0.25 = 1.7°, which matches the reset interval; and Ω × H = 1.658 × 10⁻⁵ × 0.3016 = 5.0 × 10⁻⁶ N·m, the torque we started with.

bank.q: An aircraft flying at 30 000 ft reads a DME slant range of 40 nm to a ground station near sea level. Find the ground range and comment on the error as the aircraft nears the overhead.
outline: Height in nautical miles: 30 000 ÷ 6076 = 4.94 nm
Ground range = √(40² − 4.94²) = 39.69 nm
Slant range always exceeds ground range
The error grows as ground range falls; overhead the DME still reads 4.94 nm
DME distance near the station is used with care or corrected
answer: DME measures slant range, the straight line from the aircraft to the ground transponder, not the distance over the ground. Height, slant range and ground range form a right-angled triangle with the slant range as the hypotenuse, so d = √(r² − h²) with all three in the same unit.

answer.text: Convert the height to nautical miles (1 nm = 6076 ft) and solve, taking the station near sea level:

answer: Result. The ground range is 39.69 nm. The DME over-reads by 0.31 nm, under 1%, which is negligible for en-route navigation.

answer.text: Near the overhead. Keep the height and shrink the reading:

answer: The error grows quickly as the aircraft closes on the station. From 30 nm it is still only 0.41 nm; at a reading of 5 nm the aircraft is only 0.79 nm from the station over the ground; and directly overhead the DME still reads the height, 4.94 nm, with zero ground range. A DME reading can never be less than the height above the station.

A working rule: the slant error is small when the slant range in nautical miles is at least the height in thousands of feet (here 30 nm for 30 000 ft, an error of 0.41 nm, about 1.4%). Closer in, the FMS corrects the reading with the known heights, or the crew treats DME distance as approximate.

Why it matters: a DME arc or a DME fix flown close to a station at high altitude puts the aircraft nearer the station than the reading says; for a two-DME fix, stations far away and at good cut angles are preferred.

bank.q: An aircraft is established on a 3° glide path, 5 nm (along the ground) from the point where the path meets the runway. Compute its height and state what happens to the path and the rate of descent if a 10 kt headwind develops while the needles stay centred.
outline: Height = 5 nm × 6076 ft × tan 3° = about 1592 ft
Rule of thumb: about 318 ft per nautical mile
The beam is fixed in space; a headwind lowers ground speed and so the rate of descent, not the geometry
Rate of descent ≈ 5.3 × ground speed in kt for 3°
Centring the needles keeps the aircraft on the same straight path
answer: The glide path is a fixed inclined plane in space, set by the ground antenna. On the path, height above the runway is the ground distance to the point where the path meets the runway times tan 3°.

answer.text: Height at 5 nm:
The same rule gives about 318 ft for every nautical mile, which crews use to check the profile against DME:

answer: The headwind. Take an approach airspeed of 140 kt in still air, so the ground speed is 140 kt. A 10 kt headwind develops; the airspeed stays 140 kt, so the ground speed falls to 130 kt.

answer.text: Rate of descent on a fixed slope is ground speed times the slope:
answer.pre:
rate of descent = ground speed (ft/min) × tan 3°
140 kt: 140 × 6076 ÷ 60 × 0.05241 = 743 ft/min
130 kt: 130 × 6076 ÷ 60 × 0.05241 = 690 ft/min
rule of thumb: about 5.3 × ground speed in kt (or 5 × ground speed)

answer: What happens. The path itself does not move: the beam is fixed to the ground. If the pilot kept the old 743 ft/min, the aircraft would sink below the path and the needle would show "fly up". Keeping the needles centred means reducing the rate of descent to about 690 ft/min and adding a little power to hold the airspeed. The aircraft then flies the same straight line, more slowly over the ground.

The approach also takes longer: 5 nm at 140 kt takes 2.14 min, at 130 kt 2.31 min. A tailwind does the opposite and needs a higher rate of descent, which is why a tailwind approach is harder to stabilise.

Note on the threshold: the glide path meets the runway about 300 m (984 ft) beyond the threshold, so the aircraft crosses the threshold at about 984 × 0.05241 = 52 ft, the normal threshold crossing height.
Check: 1592 ft ÷ 743 ft/min = 2.14 min, the same as 5 nm at 140 kt, so the height and the rate of descent agree.

bank.q: An accelerometer in an inertial system has a residual bias of 1 mg. Compute the velocity and position error after 100 s of pure inertial operation and explain the shape of the growth.
outline: Velocity error = b t = 0.981 m/s
Position error = ½ b t² = 49 m
Velocity error grows with t and position error with t², while t is well under the 84.4 min Schuler period
With Schuler tuning the bias error later swings with an 84.4 min period instead of growing
Sources and cures: calibration, temperature compensation, GPS updates
answer: An accelerometer with a bias reports a constant false acceleration b. The INS integrates it once into a velocity error and again into a position error. Over a short time, long before the Schuler loop acts, the errors are δv = b t and δp = ½ b t².

answer.text: Convert and compute for t = 100 s:
The shape of the growth shows in a table:

answer: Velocity error grows in proportion to time; position error grows with the square of time, so ten times longer gives a hundred times the error (0.49 m at 10 s, 49 m at 100 s).

Why the growth does not go on for ever. An INS is Schuler-tuned: its level loop has the 84.4 min period of a pendulum as long as the Earth's radius. A position error tilts the computed level frame, and the tilt feeds back a part of gravity that opposes the error. With the loop closed, an accelerometer bias gives δp = (bR ÷ g)(1 − cos ωst), where ωs = √(g ÷ R).

answer.text: For this bias:

answer: So the ½ b t² curve is the start of a Schuler swing: it holds for the first few minutes (well under 13 min), and after that the error oscillates between zero and about 12.7 km with an 84.4 min period instead of growing without bound.

Sources of such errors: bias and its turn-on repeatability, scale-factor error, axis misalignment, temperature drift, and the gravity error from a tilted platform (a tilt of 1 mrad puts 1 mg of gravity on a horizontal accelerometer).

Cures: factory calibration and temperature compensation of the sensors; ground alignment, which levels the platform and leaves a tilt that cancels the bias; and updates from GPS or other aids through a Kalman filter, which estimates the bias as a state and removes it.
Check: at 100 s the two formulas agree, 49.05 m open-loop against 48.99 m with the Schuler loop, as they must so early, and δv ÷ t = 0.981 ÷ 100 = 9.81 × 10⁻³ m/s², the bias itself.

bank.q: A satellite clock is in error by 10 ns. Compute the equivalent range error, and explain why a receiver needs four satellites rather than three.
outline: Range error = c Δt = 3 × 10⁸ × 10 × 10⁻⁹ = 3 m
Unknowns are x, y, z and the receiver clock offset, so four satellites are needed for four equations
Broadcast clock parameters correct the satellite clock but not the receiver clock
Pseudorange equation ρ = r + c δt shows the receiver clock offset entering every measurement
Geometry quality is described by dilution of precision
answer: GPS measures range by timing: the receiver multiplies the signal's travel time by the speed of light. Any timing error therefore becomes a range error of c times the timing error.

answer.text: Satellite clock error of 10 ns:
The same rule shows why clocks matter so much:

answer: Satellite clock. Each satellite carries atomic clocks, and the control segment measures their offset and broadcasts clock correction terms in the navigation message. The receiver applies them, leaving a residual of the order of a metre. A satellite clock error is common to every user of that satellite, so differential corrections also remove it.

Receiver clock. The receiver has a cheap quartz clock. An offset δt of a microsecond is common and adds 300 m to every pseudorange. So the measured quantity is a pseudorange: ρ = r + c δt, where r is the true geometric range.

Four unknowns need four equations. The receiver does not know x, y, z or δt. Each satellite gives one equation, ρi = √((xi − x)² + (yi − y)² + (zi − z)²) + c δt. Three satellites would do only if the receiver clock were perfect; with the clock unknown, four satellites are the minimum, and more give a least-squares solution and an integrity check.

answer.text: A one-dimensional model shows the idea. Two synchronised beacons 12.000 km apart; the receiver reads ρ<sub>A</sub> = 5.300 km and ρ<sub>B</sub> = 7.300 km; b = c δt:

answer: Two unknowns needed two beacons; in space there are four unknowns, so four satellites. Their geometry sets the dilution of precision (DOP), which multiplies the range error into the position error.

bank.q: A primary surveillance radar receives an echo 100 µs after transmission and works at a pulse repetition frequency of 1 kHz. Find the target range and the maximum unambiguous range.
outline: Factor of two because the pulse travels out and back
Maximum unambiguous range = c / (2 × PRF) = 150 km
Beyond that range echoes arrive after the next pulse and appear as second-trace returns
Range resolution depends on pulse width, not on PRF
answer: A primary radar measures the time between sending a pulse and hearing its echo. The pulse goes out to the target and back, so the range is half the distance light travels in that time: R = c t ÷ 2.

answer.text: Target range:

answer: The factor of two is the most common slip: without it the answer would be 30 km, twice the true range.

answer.text: Maximum unambiguous range. The next pulse leaves after the pulse repetition interval 1 ÷ PRF. An echo must return before then, or the radar times it from the wrong pulse:
Second-trace echoes. A target beyond Ru is not lost; it shows at the wrong range. A target at 180 km returns after 1.2 ms, which is 0.2 ms after the next pulse:
answer.pre:
echo time = 2 × 180 000 ÷ (3 × 10⁸) = 1.2 ms
timed from the next pulse: 1.2 − 1.0 = 0.2 ms
apparent range = 3 × 10⁸ × 0.2 × 10⁻³ ÷ 2 = 30 km

answer: Radars defeat this by changing the PRF from scan to scan (PRF stagger): a true echo stays at the same range, a second-trace echo jumps.

answer.text: The design trade-offs at a glance:

answer: Range resolution depends on the pulse width τ, not on the PRF: two targets closer than c τ ÷ 2 merge into one echo. A higher PRF puts more pulses on each target (better detection and Doppler measurement) but shortens the unambiguous range, so surveillance radars use a low PRF and several PRFs together.
Check: 15 km is less than 150 km, so the 100 µs echo is unambiguous; and 2 × 15 000 ÷ (3 × 10⁸) = 100 µs, the measured delay.

bank.q: A scalar Kalman filter has a predicted position variance P = 100 m² and a GPS measurement variance R = 25 m². Compute the Kalman gain, the updated variance and the weight given to each source.
outline: Updated variance = (1 − K) P = 0.2 × 100 = 20 m²
Measurement is trusted with weight 0.8, prediction with weight 0.2
The update can never be worse than the better of the two inputs
In the vector case K is a matrix and P is a covariance matrix
answer: In one dimension the Kalman update blends a prediction (variance P) with a measurement (variance R). The gain K is the fraction of the innovation, measurement minus prediction, that is added to the prediction.

answer.text: Gain and new variance:

answer: Weights. The updated estimate is x ← x + K (z − x) = (1 − K) x + K z. So the GPS measurement gets weight K = 0.8 and the prediction 1 − K = 0.2. The weights are inversely proportional to the variances: 25 m² is four times smaller than 100 m², so the GPS is trusted four times as much (0.8 ÷ 0.2 = 4).

answer.text: With numbers: the INS predicts 1000 m along track, the GPS reads 1050 m:
answer.pre:
innovation y = 1050 − 1000 = 50 m
correction K y = 0.8 × 50 = 40 m
blend x = 1000 + 40 = 1040 m

answer.text: How K moves with the inputs (R = 25 m² fixed):

answer: A confident prediction (small P) gets a small gain and the measurement barely moves it; an uncertain prediction (large P, after a GPS outage for example) gets a gain near 1 and the measurement takes over.
Never worse than the better input. In one dimension 1 ÷ Pnew = 1 ÷ P + 1 ÷ R, so the new variance is smaller than both P and R: 20 m² is less than 25 m². Information adds.

The vector case. In a GPS-INS filter the state x is a vector (position, velocity, attitude, sensor biases), P is a covariance matrix, and K = P Hᵀ (H P Hᵀ + R)⁻¹ is a matrix that also spreads a position correction into velocity and bias corrections through the off-diagonal terms of P.
Check: 1 ÷ 100 + 1 ÷ 25 = 0.01 + 0.04 = 0.05, and 1 ÷ 0.05 = 20 m², the same new variance by a second route.

bank.q: Explain why neither a stand-alone inertial navigation system nor a stand-alone GPS receiver is satisfactory for a long flight, and how loosely coupled GPS-INS integration solves both problems.
outline: INS: self-contained, smooth, high short-term accuracy; with Schuler tuning a gyro bias still makes position error ramp up without bound
GPS: bounded error, but noisy, low update rate, and can be lost or jammed
Fusion: filter estimates INS error states and feeds corrections back
GPS provides the long-term reference, INS bridges between updates and rejects noise
Feedback of corrections keeps the INS error small so the model stays linear
Bridging also gives continuity during a coasting period; describe the covariance behaviour
answer: For a long flight the navigation solution must be accurate, smooth, available at a high rate, and still there when one sensor fails. Neither an INS nor a GPS receiver does all of this alone; their errors are complementary.

answer.text: The INS alone. It is self-contained, cannot be jammed, gives attitude and velocity at 50 Hz or more, and is very smooth. But it integrates its sensor errors. With Schuler tuning an accelerometer bias gives a bounded 84.4 min swing, while a gyro bias makes the position error ramp up. For a gyro bias of 0.01 °/h:
answer.pre:
ε = 0.01 °/h = 4.848 × 10⁻⁸ rad/s
Δp = R ε (t − sin(ω<sub>s</sub>t) ÷ ω<sub>s</sub>)
at 1 h: 1353 m (1.35 km); at 2 h: 2.11 km
long-term ramp R ε = 0.309 m/s, about 0.6 nm every hour

answer.text: GPS alone. Its error is bounded and does not grow with time: with a range error (UERE) of 5.0 m and HDOP 1.8 the horizontal error is about 1.8 × 5.0 = 9.0 m, now or ten hours later. But it is noisy from fix to fix, updates only at 1 to 10 Hz, gives no attitude, and the signal arrives at about −130 dBm, so it can be blocked by aircraft manoeuvres, jammed or spoofed.

answer: Loosely coupled integration. The GPS receiver computes its own position and velocity. A Kalman filter compares them with the INS solution; the difference (the innovation) drives an error-state filter whose states are the INS errors: position, velocity and attitude errors plus gyro and accelerometer biases, typically 15 states.

answer.text: The loop, step by step:

head: Step
What happens
rows: The INS runs at full rate; the filter propagates its error estimate and grows P by the process noise Q
At each GPS fix the innovation y = z − H x is formed from GPS minus INS position and velocity
K = P Hᵀ (H P Hᵀ + R)⁻¹ weights the innovation; the error estimate and P are corrected
The estimated position, velocity and attitude errors are removed from the INS, and the bias estimates correct the sensors

answer: What each sensor gives the other. GPS is the long-term reference that stops the INS error ramp and calibrates its biases. The INS fills the gaps between GPS fixes, smooths GPS noise, gives attitude, and keeps navigating when GPS is lost. Feeding the corrections back keeps the INS errors small, so the linear error model inside the filter stays valid.

answer.text: Coasting through an outage. After an update P = 20 m². GPS is lost for 30 s and each one-second predict step adds Q = 4 m²:

answer: During the outage the covariance grows and the gain rises (0.444 without the outage, 0.848 after it), so the first fix after reacquisition pulls the estimate firmly back. Because the biases were calibrated before the outage, the INS drifts far less than an uncalibrated one would.

Loose coupling is simple and keeps the GPS receiver independent, but it needs four satellites for a GPS fix. Tightly coupled integration feeds raw pseudoranges into the filter, so even two or three satellites still help, and the INS can aid the receiver's tracking loops.

Check: the integrated error stays near the GPS level of a few metres (σ = 4.61 m after the outage) instead of the INS ramp of 1.35 km at one hour, and the INS keeps the solution continuous through the 30 s gap.

bank.q: Classify the error sources that limit GPS accuracy and match each one with the correction technique used in practice.
outline: Satellite clock and orbit (ephemeris) errors, including the selective availability of the past; corrected by broadcast parameters and differential corrections
Ionosphere: dispersive, corrected by dual frequency, ionospheric models or SBAS
Troposphere: non-dispersive, corrected by a model using surface pressure, temperature and humidity
Receiver and antenna: multipath, noise, antenna phase centre; corrected by antenna siting, choke-ring antennas and filtering
Dilution of precision amplifies all of the above by poor satellite geometry
RAIM and augmentation systems check integrity, not just accuracy
answer: GPS position error comes from errors in each pseudorange, multiplied by the geometry of the satellites. The range errors fall into four families: satellite clock and orbit, ionosphere, troposphere, and local effects at the receiver. Each family has a different physical cause, so each has a different cure.

Clocks and orbits. The satellite clock and the broadcast orbit are never perfect; the residuals after the broadcast corrections are about a metre each. Until May 2000 selective availability added deliberate clock dithering of tens of metres; it is now off. Differential GPS and SBAS remove these errors because they are the same for every nearby user.

Ionosphere. The delay is 40.3 × TEC ÷ f², so it depends on frequency: the ionosphere is dispersive. That is the key to its cure. A dual-frequency receiver measures the same range on L1 and L5 and solves for the delay; a single-frequency receiver uses the broadcast model, which removes only about half. SBAS (GAGAN, WAAS, EGNOS) broadcast a grid of measured delays. Example: 12.0 m on L1 becomes 12.0 × (1575.42 ÷ 1176.45)² = 21.5 m on L5, and the difference between them reveals both.

Troposphere. The neutral air delays all frequencies equally (non-dispersive), so dual frequency does nothing. About 2.5 m at the zenith, it grows as 1 ÷ sin(elevation): 2.5 ÷ sin 10° = 14.4 m at 10°. It is corrected with a model using surface pressure, temperature and humidity, and by an elevation mask.

Local effects. Multipath (reflections from the airframe or nearby buildings), receiver noise and antenna phase-centre variation are unique to each receiver, so differential corrections cannot remove them. Cures are good antenna siting, choke-ring antennas, narrow correlators and carrier smoothing.

answer.text: Putting numbers on it. Illustrative 1-sigma residuals for a single-frequency receiver after the broadcast corrections, combined by root-sum-square into the user equivalent range error (UERE):

head: Source
Residual (m)
Correction used in practice
rows: Broadcast ephemeris; differential or precise orbits
Model from pressure, temperature, humidity and elevation
Antenna siting, choke-ring antennas, narrow correlators

answer.text: Geometry multiplies UERE into position error:
answer.pre:
single frequency: σ<sub>h</sub> = HDOP × UERE = 1.8 × 4.40 = 7.9 m
dual frequency (ionosphere residual 0.5 m): UERE = 1.90 m, σ<sub>h</sub> = 1.8 × 1.90 = 3.4 m

answer: The ionosphere dominates a single-frequency budget, which is why the move to dual-frequency L1/L5 avionics and SBAS matters most for aviation.

Dilution of precision is not an error source: it is the geometry factor. Satellites bunched in one part of the sky give a large DOP and stretch every range error; a multi-constellation receiver sees more satellites and lowers it.

Integrity, not just accuracy. A satellite fault can give a large error without warning. RAIM checks the consistency of redundant pseudoranges: five satellites are needed to detect a faulty one and six to exclude it. SBAS also sends integrity flags. Aviation needs both a small error and a guarantee that it is small.
Check: √(1.1² + 0.8² + 4.0² + 0.5² + 1.0² + 0.5²) = √19.35 = 4.40 m, and removing the ionosphere term almost entirely cuts UERE by more than half, to 1.90 m.

bank.q: Describe the modes of a ground proximity warning system, and argue why the reactive modes had to be supplemented by a look-ahead terrain function.
outline: Reactive modes use radio altitude, barometric rate and the ILS: excessive descent rate, excessive terrain closure, height loss after take-off, unsafe terrain clearance, excessive deviation below the glide path, callouts, windshear
Warning envelopes widen as height above ground falls and as speed rises
Reactive warning fires only when the terrain is already under the aircraft
Look-ahead modes compare GPS or FMS position and projected path against a terrain and obstacle database
Database gives alerts tens of seconds earlier, plus a visual terrain display
Limits: database currency, position error, false alerts near steep terrain
answer: Controlled flight into terrain (CFIT) is a serviceable aircraft flown into the ground with the crew unaware. A ground proximity warning system (GPWS) warns from the aircraft's height above the ground and how that height is changing.

answer.text: The reactive GPWS modes and their inputs:

head: Mode
Detects
Main inputs
Aural call
rows: Barometric sink rate against radio altitude
Rate of change of radio altitude
Height loss after take-off or go-around
Barometric height lost, against radio altitude
Too close to the ground, not in landing configuration
Radio altitude, gear and flap position, speed
TOO LOW GEAR, TOO LOW FLAPS, TOO LOW TERRAIN
Excessive deviation below the glide path
ILS glide path deviation, radio altitude

answer: Envelopes. Each mode is a boundary on a graph of radio altitude against a rate. A sink rate that is normal at 2000 ft is dangerous at 300 ft, so the warning boundary allows less rate the lower the aircraft is; Mode 2 widens its envelope at higher speed because the ground is reached sooner. Each mode gives a caution first and a PULL UP warning if the condition worsens.

Why reactive is not enough. Every reactive mode uses the radio altimeter, which looks straight down. It cannot see terrain ahead. Against a gently rising slope Mode 2 sees the closure and warns, typically 10 to 30 s before impact. Against a steep ridge or a cliff the ground below does not rise until the aircraft is over it, so there is no closure rate to see, and the first warning can come too late to climb. The aircraft can be on a normal descent, in landing configuration, and still be flying at a mountain.

answer.text: A worked case. An aircraft at 5000 ft descends at 1500 ft/min at 240 kt over ground at 1000 ft. A ridge with its top at 3000 ft begins 8 nm ahead:
answer.pre:
time to the ridge = 8 ÷ 240 h = 120 s
altitude then = 5000 − 1500 × 2 = 2000 ft, below the 3000 ft top: the path hits the ridge face
radio altitude 30 s before impact = 2750 − 1000 = 1750 ft, sinking at an ordinary 1500 ft/min
so no reactive mode is triggered: the ground below is flat

answer.text: The look-ahead function. TAWS (enhanced GPWS) keeps the reactive modes and adds forward-looking terrain avoidance (FLTA). It projects the flight path from GNSS or FMS position, track, ground speed and vertical speed, and compares it with a terrain and obstacle database. In the case above:
answer.pre:
caution, 60 s before impact: t = 60 s, 3500 ft, 4.0 nm from the ridge, "CAUTION TERRAIN"
warning, 30 s before impact: t = 90 s, 2750 ft, 2.0 nm out, "TERRAIN, PULL UP"
climb needed to clear the top by 500 ft: 750 ft in 30 s = 1500 ft/min
after a 5 s delay: 750 ft in 25 s = 1800 ft/min

answer: TAWS also gives a premature descent alert (too low for the distance to the runway, the case Mode 4 misses in landing configuration) and a terrain display coloured by height relative to the aircraft, so the crew sees the threat before any alert. Class A TAWS, for larger airliners, has FLTA, the premature descent alert, the display and the full reactive modes; Class B, for smaller aircraft, has FLTA, the premature descent alert and fewer reactive modes.

Limits of the look-ahead. The database must be current (a new tower or cable is invisible until added), position error or a wrong altimeter setting shifts the prediction, and steep approaches into terrain-ringed airfields can give nuisance alerts, which crews may inhibit only by procedure. The reactive modes stay as an independent backup that needs no database.

Judgement. The reactive modes answer "is the ground below too close or coming up too fast?"; FLTA answers "will my path meet terrain ahead?". Only the second question protects against a steep face, and it gives a minute of warning instead of seconds, which is why the reactive modes had to be supplemented, not replaced.
Check: at the warning the aircraft has 30 s and needs 750 ft, 750 ÷ 0.5 min = 1500 ft/min, exactly its present descent rate reversed; every second of delay raises the needed climb rate.

bank.q: Compare a VOR/DME area-navigation fix with an ILS approach, in terms of the lines of position used and the accuracy the operation demands.
outline: VOR/DME gives rho-theta: one bearing line and one range circle from the same station
DME alone gives a circle; a second DME gives a circle whose crossing is a fix, with poor geometry near the baseline
ILS gives two planes of constant angle, not range, so accuracy is angular and tightens as the aircraft nears the runway
En-route accuracy is of the order of a nautical mile; ILS has to keep the aircraft within metres of the centreline at the threshold
Both depend on correct receiver tuning, identification and monitoring
Why angular guidance is the right choice for the final approach
answer: Both give a position from radio lines of position, but they are built for different jobs: VOR/DME area navigation keeps an aircraft near a route of its own choosing en route, while ILS keeps it on one fixed path down to a runway.

VOR/DME lines of position. A VOR gives a bearing line (a radial) from the station; a DME gives a range circle. From one co-located VOR/DME the two cross at 90°, the rho-theta fix. An RNAV computer converts this to position and flies to waypoints that need not lie on any radial. A DME/DME fix uses two range circles from different stations, with a good cut only when the stations are well apart in bearing; near the baseline joining them the cut angle closes and the fix degrades.

answer.text: VOR/DME accuracy is angular for the bearing. A bearing error spreads with distance from the station:
answer.pre:
cross-track error = distance × tan(bearing error)
50 nm, 1°: 50 × tan 1° = 0.87 nm (1616 m)
50 nm, 2°: 50 × tan 2° = 1.75 nm
DME along-track error: about 0.2 nm, nearly constant with range

answer: So VOR/DME accuracy is of the order of a nautical mile at typical en-route distances. That is enough for en-route RNAV, whose specifications ask the aircraft to stay within 5 nm (RNAV 5) or 1 nm (RNAV 1) of the route 95% of the time.

ILS lines of position. ILS measures two angles from the runway, not ranges: the localizer gives a vertical plane through the centreline and the glide path an inclined plane at 3°. Their intersection is the approach line. Range comes only from markers or DME, and it matters little, because the guidance is a line to follow, not a point to find.

answer.text: ILS accuracy tightens as the runway nears, because a fixed angle covers fewer metres closer in. With a localizer 3300 m from the threshold (half-angle 1.82°) and a 3° glide path:

head: Where
Localizer full scale (each side)
Glide path full scale (above)
rows: 5 nm from where the path meets the runway
1 nm from where the path meets the runway

answer: The final approach needs this: the aircraft must arrive within a few metres of the centreline and a few feet of the right height at the decision height, and an autoland must touch down on the centreline. A VOR bearing error that grows with distance from a station cannot give that; an angle measured from the runway itself gives errors that shrink to metres exactly where they matter.

answer.text: Side by side:

head: VOR/DME RNAV
ILS
rows: Radial line and range circle (or two circles)
About 1 nm en route, worse far from the station
Monitors shut a faulty beam off; ident check

answer: Common requirements. Both depend on correct tuning and identification by Morse code, and on monitors; neither may be used if the ident is missing. Both suffer from site errors and reflections, which is why ILS critical areas are kept clear in low visibility.

Judgement. Range-and-bearing fixing suits en-route flight, where any point may be a waypoint and a nautical mile is acceptable. Angular guidance from the runway suits the final approach, where only one path matters and the error must shrink to metres at the threshold. So angular guidance is the right choice for the last few miles.

Check: the localizer full-scale offset grows in proportion to distance, 318 m at 10 km against 105 m at 3.3 km (ratio 3.03, as 10 ÷ 3.3); and the glide path band shrinks fivefold from 5 nm to 1 nm (372 ft to 74 ft).

glossary.def: The closeness of a reported position to the true position, expressed in metres or nautical miles.
The closeness of repeated readings of the same true value to each other, which can be good even when accuracy is poor.
The curve or straight line on which one measurement is constant, so it contains the true position.
The point where two or more lines of position cross, taken as the aircraft's position.
The horizontal direction from the aircraft to a station, measured clockwise from north in degrees.
The direction in which the aircraft nose points, measured clockwise from north in degrees.
A Cartesian frame with its origin at the Earth's centre and axes fixed to the rotating Earth.
A navigation frame at the aircraft with axes pointing north, east and down.
The curve traced by points whose distances to two fixed stations differ by a constant amount.
Distance Measuring Equipment: an interrogator in the aircraft and a transponder on the ground that together give slant range in nautical miles from round-trip time.
The ILS ground beam that gives left-right guidance relative to the runway centreline.
The ILS ground beam that gives up-down guidance along the approach path, normally 3°.
The steady turning of a spinning axis at right angles to an applied torque, at a rate set by the torque and the spin momentum.
A short-lived wobble of a gyroscope's spin axis about its steady direction after a disturbance.
A pivoted ring that lets an instrument or platform rotate about one axis independently of its mount.
A sensor that measures specific force along one sensitive axis, that is, acceleration minus gravity.
Designing the inertial platform loop to have an 84.4 min period so that horizontal acceleration does not build a growing tilt error.
The apparent satellite-to-receiver range obtained from signal travel time before the receiver clock offset is estimated and removed.
The set of orbital parameters broadcast by a navigation satellite so a receiver can compute its position.
A factor that amplifies range errors into position errors because of the geometry of the visible satellites.
A recursive estimator that combines a predicted state with a new measurement, weighting each by its covariance.
A surveillance service in which an aircraft broadcasts its identity, position and velocity, derived from its own navigation systems.
A frequency-modulated radar that measures height above the terrain directly beneath the aircraft.
Terrain Awareness and Warning System: equipment that alerts the crew to terrain or obstacle conflict, using radio altitude and a terrain database.
